POST GUIDELINES

The following aren't rules, just guidelines. We won't ban you for going against them, but your post may be deleted as spam:

1.) PLEASE scroll down at least a day or two worth of posts and make sure your link is unique, and PLEASE do not post an article or link that you have posted 5 times elsewhere across voat, because it makes you look like you're pushing an agenda.

I really like to learn about history. If we can truly grasp the topic, I believe it is possible for men to rediscover true masculinity, find out exactly why Cultural Marxists, SJWs, and similar are trying to hide, and perhaps use some of the best ideas in history to create a path forward for men today.

How to read history

Probably the worst way to understand history is to do so in the manner you were taught in school. You might remember the dreadful topic: remembering dates and times and the textbook interpretation of events. I would go so far as to call this negative knowledge, you have to unlearn what you 'learned' in school before you can make any progress. Instead, it is better to think of societies in hisory much like how we look at society today: many different factions of people, each moving in their own direction, some succeeding more than others.

This approach to history makes the topic that much more interesting, and approachable. It quickly becomes clear that this is not the first time in history that truth has been shut out of places of higher learning, that social institutions have been attacked and redefined, and so on. Indeed, it brings on to realize that here, right now, you are standing in a very significant part of history, and have the opportunity to insert yourself into it. If you read what past men have done, you may just be able to duplicate their successes.

Finally, when reading history, one interesting observation I run into, is the notion that "the best way to date the past by by its perception of the future." We have no idea what the future will bring, we do know that many spectacular failures began when a society declared itself perfect. This is an important step in learning humility; as a scientist I wish for the best but I cannot put my faith in humanity teching its way out of every inconvenience.

Using history to rediscover manliness

It is also important to understand that certain ideas we see today are in fact repeats of the same idea in another period of history, which allows us to understand the present that much better. My father used to call this "learning from other's mistakes," but indeed, we can also learn from other men's successes as well. If you read about great men in history, you can Find what kind of great man you could emulate, and in so doing, become one yourself.

This practice actually has a saying attached, "We are dwarves standing on the shoulders of giants."

Using history to fight the present ignorance

If you get into history, you will find very quickly that the trip from the past to the present is very different than what you have been taught. This is a case of separating the data from the interpretation again.

The modern-day Cultural Marxists know very well that history testifies against the viability of their movement. Feminism has been tried, and found to lead to injustice and ruin. Demagougery disguised as democracy has also been tried, and found to lead to ruin. No advanced civilization has ever gotten started without a strong institution of marriage. Among much more evidence pointing to the inconsistency and inevitable failure of an ideology that tries to make women men, and declare broken families whole. This is why the Cultural Marxist must lie, primarily by spinning the narrative of progress: all history only moves forward, and therfore anything in the past is "outdated."

To counter this, ask questions about whether the Cultural Marxist is aware of what family structures look like at the rise and fall of other societies. Ask what the implication is of most medieval scholars being given positions in the Church (meaning that "the Church" was as much about contemporary academics as it was about religion), or that many of the theological innovations in the last 500 years came from people outside the official Church, working their way in through each revival. We need to be unashamed of our heritage, who we are, and further, we need to form our identity out of the best ideas of great men.

The Suffering: Prison is Hell.

Such an amazing game, they did a great job and creating a really creepy atmosphere. There's a lot of darkness and claustrophobic corridors. You never know what's going to pop out from around the corner, or ceiling of that puddle of blood on the ground. They were one of the early games to incorporate a moral system, so the ending and some of the dialogue drastically changes based on your decisions in the game.

The monsters are all unique and frighteningly detailed. From the first Slayers to the last boss fight. They did a great job on making each monster different.

The storyline, very well done. It draws you in as you play and unlock or discover things from your past. They did an amazing job creating centuries of history on carnate island. From puritan to slave trades to ww2, the cold war through present times.

The characters are quite exceptional although some could have been done much better. You play as Torque, a convicted murderer who killed his family but can't remember the whole thing. Chlem and his calm methodical plan to escape by sea. Horace and Hermes and their cat and mouse games with you until their second demise. Dr killjoy and his batshit insanity. Killjoys asylum is probably one of my favorite parts of the game. And of course the endearing Sergei. A guard who abandons his post when shit goes down, to sneak off into a haunted asylum and smoke weed while drinking beer. He's always been my favorite. And someday buddy, I'll figure out how to replace your broken hooka with the one from your stash.

Overall midway did an incredible job on this game, you can tell the developer's had a lot of fun creating this masterpiece. Sadly the second one, while improving the game mechanics greatly, was not able to capture what made the first game such a great cult classic. The original Half Life is one of the worst games I've ever played. The enemies in that game are ridiculous. I couldn't even force myself to play blue shift, or the other one. At least half life 2 was good.

Consider the Roman household slaves: they were fed, clothed, had roof over their heads and worked for their owners. They had to ask their owner for permission for virtually anything and everything. While many people will disagree with this comparison, how is that any different from regular employees today? We are paid in currency which is then exchanged for food, shelter, clothing. For most people, their salary is just enough to cover these things - and for that, they work 10-12 hours a day. They cannot go for a vacation without the approval from their boss and even if they get it, there's the issue of the salary again - not earning nearly enough to go somewhere interesting. It's another form of permission. I don't want to go deeper on this (since that's not the point of this post) but my opinion is that our modern civilization has created a legalized, institutionalized version of slavery. We are led to believe that we are fre while we really are not - instead of direcly being owned by someone, a middleman was added - money. Corporations own us and money is used to keep us in check.

So these corporations that make us work 8 (if we're lucky) - 10 (pretty standard) - ?? hours every day don't really leave us with much free time. Add the time it takes you to commute (2 hours/day on average) and you're lucky to get home before sunset. So you come back from your underpaid job where you spend most of your waking hours - and you go and cook a healthy meal? Yes, I didn't think so. You are tired, want to finally spend time with your family and in no mood for BS. So you eat cheap, processed, pre-made food that you can easily nuke in the microwave. Beautiful, tasty, hyperpalatable, comforting food.

Corporations spend a lot of money on marketing hyperpalatable food. It's no secret in the PC gaming industry that psychologists are hired to make a game addictive. I have no illusions that scientists are hired in the food industry to make food more addictive (hello, HFCS and other refined sugars). How else would corporations make money? A recent study confirms that a person addicted to refined sugar has worse cravings than a crack addict. There are physical withdrawal symptoms. If that's not scary, I don't know what is.

Your body goes through physiological changes that correspond to your diet. It's so easy to say "eat less" when that leaves people literally strugglig to get through the day because of the lack of energy. It's so easy to say "don't drink soda" when your brain screams for it's sugars and your body is reacting with physical pain. If you read up on the keto diet, which changes the way your body gets energy, you will see that there is a period at the beginning where people are physically ill. That's how bad the food we generally eat is. And that's how strong a change is needed.

I do not want to disregard personal responsibility. However, I want to point out how ridiculously easy it is to get into a chicken-egg loop that doesn't end well for you. Eating healthy food is a time and money investment very people can afford. Any good fitness couch will tell you that it's less about how much you excercise and more about what you eat. People trying paleo or keto (if they can afford it) loose weight without even lifting up their ass from their couch. But not everyone can afford that luxury. Combined with the advertisement that has been tailored to be as appealing as possible and food that's been made addictive and hyperpalatable, the corporations are the main culprits behind the obesity pandemic the world is seeing today.
Some thoughts on the obesity epidemic

That's a rather depressing speech you have there. Unfortunately, that's what a good chunk of the populace believe. However, that's just like, your opinion, man.

Yes, a good portion of our day is dictated by "the man" and we're constantly being marketed to. We're led to believe that processed, happy, easy food is all we have time for and what we can afford. That's absolutely not true. Even in my 16 hour work day life I have time on Sundays to prepare well balanced meals for the week. Yes, it takes between 2-4 hours, but this bit of preparation not only reduces time, but costs less. Chicken and pork are cheap. Vegetables, within reason/season are cheap. Legumes are exceptionally cheap and healthy.

It is perfectly viable to eat healthy and exercise in today's busy 10 hours a day world. You need only get past what you believe you can't do and focus on what you can.

I disagree. My shopping budget increased 100% when I switched to non-processed food. And I was shopping smart. It goes up even more if you go paleo/keto. I have no other argument to give you, it's just economic reality in my corner of planet. So just imagine me quoting the Dude as well :)
